newsitem.title: USA: Deliberations begin in murder trial of ex-soldier.
newsitem.headline: Deliberations begin in murder trial of ex-soldier.

text.p: A North Carolina jury Tuesday ended its first day of deliberations in the case of a white former U.S. Army paratrooper charged with murdering a black couple in 1995.
After nearly three weeks of testimony, the case of James Burmeister, 21, who has been linked to a white supremacist group, was turned over to the jury Tuesday afternoon.
Deliberations stopped about an hour later when the panel sent the judge a note asking to examine clothes worn by Burmeister and co-defendant Malcolm Wright the night of the shootings.
A DNA expert testified during the prosecution's case that blood on Burmeister's clothing matched that of victims Jackie Burden, 27, and Michael James, 36.

Prosecutors plan to seek the death penalty if a guilty verdict is returned on first-degree murder charges for the deaths of Burden and James, who were shot at close range as they walked in a neighbourhood here Dec. 7, 1995.
Burmeister has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Fayetteville adjoins the U.S. Army's Fort Bragg military installation, home to the elite 82nd Airborne Division, and Burmeister and two fellow soldiers were drinking in a bar there before the murders.
During closing arguments earlier Tuesday, prosecutors reviewed evidence and ridiculed the defence's contention that no one knows what happened because no eyewitnesses testified.

"You heard the despicable and disgusting words," said prosecutor Calvin Colyer, referring to testimony that Burmeister listened to music with racist lyrics and even joked that by killing blacks he had performed "community service."

The defence argued that the state put on a weak case and attempted to divert attention to co-defendant Wright, 22. "Malcolm Wright was calling the shots. Malcolm Wright had killed before," defence lawyer Carl Ivarrson said.

After leaving the bar, Burmeister, Wright and Randy Meadows, another white former soldier, drove to the area where the couple was killed. Meadows, who confessed to driving the car and testified against Burmeister, said he heard six gunshots after Burmeister and Wright got out of the car.

He also said Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web" tattoo, a skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a gay or black person. White supremacist and bomb-making literature and a Nazi flag were found at Burmeister's trailer.
But lead prosecutor Edward Grannis said: "What we have in this courtroom is one of the two predators, and he's guilty."
Wright, of Lexington, Kentucky, will be tried in March on charges of murder and conspiracy to commit murder. He also faces the death penalty.
